title: The Senate AI Committee Picks a Lane — and the Rest of the Agenda Waits

posts.text:
South Carolina's Senate Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence held its first meeting on Sept. 16 and made an important choice early: it will limit its work to how AI is incorporated into state government.

That's a defensible starting point. It's also much narrower than the questions circulating around it this week — AI in political ads, what data government can collect, AI in K-12 curriculum, data centers and energy. Legislative staff told members that 33 states have adopted an AI definition in law and South Carolina is among the 17 that have not. Of roughly 31 AI-related bills last session, two became law, both on criminal justice matters.

The committee is scheduled to run through the summer of 2028, with a final report targeted by then; members said they hope to have recommendations ready about a year from now, ahead of the 2028 session.

Our read: the gap between the breadth of the questions and the state's limited standing capacity is the real story, and it argues for building durable institutional learning rather than waiting on a single report. Written public comment goes to AIcommittee@scsenate.gov.

Full brief from the South Carolina Artificial Intelligence Observatory below.

#SouthCarolina #AIPolicy

South Carolina's new Senate AI committee met for the first time on Sept. 16 and narrowed its focus to how AI fits inside state government. Meanwhile, lawmakers are drafting a bill on government data collection, a House panel is looking at AI in K-12, and there are still no broad state rules for AI in campaign ads. Our weekly brief walks through what happened and what we're watching.
